title: Miso Butter Salmon with Asparagus
excerpt: Honolulu weeknight miso-butter salmon with asparagus. White miso, butter, Times/Foodland fish counter. Kitchen-estimate macros. No rice.
html:
This is a twenty-minute Times or Foodland weeknight plate: salmon under a white-miso butter, asparagus in the same skillet. The usual Honolulu salmon dinner wants a sweet glaze and a scoop of rice. Skip both. The miso is salty and savory. The butter carries it. The asparagus takes the pan drippings.

I’m Mark. I cook this when I want fish on the table without standing over a poke bowl. Ask for wild salmon at the counter when they have it; farmed works if wild is out. Label-check the miso — some tubs hide sugar. If the ingredient list reads like candy, put it back and grab a plain shiro miso.

Yield: 2 servings  |  Prep: 8 minutes  |  Cook: 12 minutes  |  Total: about 20 minutes

Hawaii Grocery Notes

  • Times / Foodland: salmon fillets at the fish counter — wild if they have it, farmed only if wild is out. I want firm flesh, not a sad thawed tray. Bunched asparagus. Butter. White (shiro) miso in the refrigerated Asian aisle or near tofu. Fresh ginger, garlic, green onion.
  • Costco: big packs of frozen salmon portions work if you thaw them overnight in the fridge. Butter. Asparagus when they have it. Miso is hit-or-miss; I usually buy the tub at Times.
  • Don Quijote: more miso brands, ginger, chili pepper water, sometimes better asparagus bunches. Walk past the sweet teriyaki glazes and the bottled “miso marinade” with sugar listed second.
  • White miso only for this plate. Red miso is too aggressive for a quick butter sauce unless you cut it hard. No honey, no mirin glaze, no pineapple.

Ingredients

  • 2 salmon fillets (about 6 oz / 170 g each), skin on or off, patted dry — wild if possible, farmed if that is what is fresh
  • Kosher salt and black pepper
  • 1 tablespoon avocado oil (or light olive oil), divided
  • 1 bunch asparagus (about 12–16 oz), tough ends snapped off
  • 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened
  • 1½ tablespoons white (shiro) miso — label-check for added sugar
  • 1 teaspoon grated fresh ginger
  • 1 small garlic clove, minced or grated
  • 1–2 teaspoons water, to loosen the miso butter if needed
  • Optional: 1 green onion, sliced
  • Optional: chili pepper water or a squeeze of lemon at the table (not cooked into the butter)

Instructions

  1. Heat the oven to 425°F if you want a finish in the oven, or stay on the stovetop the whole way. Stir the softened butter, miso, ginger, and garlic into a paste. If it is stiff, mash in 1–2 teaspoons water until it spreads. Taste a dab — it should be salty and savory, not sweet. If it tastes sweet, your miso has sugar; stop and get a cleaner tub.
  2. Season the salmon lightly with salt and pepper. Remember the miso is already salty. Toss the asparagus with about ½ tablespoon of the oil, a pinch of salt, and black pepper.
  3. Heat a wide oven-safe skillet over medium-high. Add the remaining oil. Salmon in, presentation side down (skin up if skin-on). Sear 3–4 minutes until a crust forms. Flip.
  4. Spread the miso butter over the top of each fillet. Scatter the asparagus around the fish in a single layer. If the pan is crowded, pull the asparagus to a second skillet — crowded spears steam and go limp.
  5. Stovetop path: drop the heat to medium. Cover loosely 5–7 minutes until the salmon is just opaque and flakes, and the asparagus is tender-crisp. Oven path: slide the skillet into the 425°F oven for 5–7 minutes instead. Do not cook the salmon to chalk.
  6. Spoon any melted miso butter from the pan over the fillets. Green onion on top. Chili pepper water or lemon at the table. Eat it as the plate — no rice scoop.

Kitchen-Estimate Macros (per serving)

Kitchen estimates only, not lab-tested. Calculated for 1 of 2 servings (one 6 oz salmon fillet, half the miso butter, half the bunch of asparagus). Salmon fat varies by cut; I used a typical Atlantic fillet.

Notes

  • Hidden sugar: bottled miso marinades, mirin-heavy glazes, honey-miso recipes, and some white miso tubs. Shoyu is fine as a table splash. Sweet chili sauce does not belong here.
  • Skin-on fillets crisp better if you start skin-side down; for this miso-butter top, I still start presentation-side down so the butter sits on the cooked side. Either way works.
  • If asparagus is woody mid-summer, peel the lower stems or switch to broccolini. Same cook time.
  • Leftover salmon is fine cold the next day. Reheating past medium turns it dry — eat leftovers as a cold plate with the leftover spears.
  • Same weeknight fish window as the pan-seared ahi with ginger-garlic butter. Buy whichever looks better at the counter.

— Mark Souza
Honolulu

title: Watercress, Bacon, and Eggs (No Rice)
excerpt: Watercress in Honolulu is not a garnish. It is a bunch from Foodland that wilts in bacon fat and still tastes like a stream. The usual plate is watercress, bacon or Portuguese sausage, eggs, and two scoops of rice. This is the same plate without the rice. The greens take the bacon fat. That is […]
html:
Watercress in Honolulu is not a garnish. It is a bunch from Foodland that wilts in bacon fat and still tastes like a stream. The usual plate is watercress, bacon or Portuguese sausage, eggs, and two scoops of rice. This is the same plate without the rice. The greens take the bacon fat. That is the whole trick.

I’m Mark. I cook this as a late breakfast most days I can find a decent bunch. Summer through early fall the watercress is actually good. If the stems look tired, skip it and make the Portuguese sausage skillet instead. I am not forcing a sad bag of salad into a Honolulu breakfast.

Yield: 2 servings  |  Prep: 10 minutes  |  Cook: 15 minutes  |  Total: about 25 minutes

Hawaii Grocery Notes

  • Foodland / Times: bunched watercress in produce (look for perky stems, not yellow leaves). Eggs. Thick-cut bacon if they have it.
  • Costco: eggs, bacon in the big pack. Watercress is hit-or-miss; I usually get the bunch at Foodland.
  • Don Quijote: bacon, eggs, chili pepper water, sometimes watercress. Skip the pre-washed “spring mix” swap. That is a different dish.
  • Local watercress (Sumida and the other valley growers when you see the name) is the point. Mainland clamshell baby watercress is too mild and too expensive for this.

Ingredients

  • 1 large bunch watercress (about 8–10 oz), washed well, thick woody ends trimmed, cut into 3-inch lengths
  • 6 slices bacon
  • 4 large eggs
  • Black pepper
  • Optional: chili pepper water or a splash of shoyu at the table
  • Optional: 2 oz leftover kalua pig, warmed in the bacon fat before the greens
  • Salt only after tasting — bacon is already salty

Instructions

  1. Wash the watercress in a deep bowl. Sand hides in the stems. Drain well. You want it wet enough to steam a little, not dripping.
  2. Cook the bacon in a wide skillet over medium until the fat renders and the slices are browned, 8–10 minutes. Transfer bacon to a plate. Leave about 2 tablespoons of fat in the pan. Pour off extra but keep it; you may want a spoonful back.
  3. Raise the heat to medium-high. Add the watercress. It will look like too much. Toss in the fat 1–2 minutes until the leaves wilt and the stems are tender-crisp and still bright. If the pan is dry, a spoon of reserved fat. Do not cook it to army green.
  4. Push the greens to the sides. Crack the eggs into the open space, or make wells. Cook until the whites set and the yolks are how you eat them. I like the edges a little crisp and the yolks runny so they sauce the greens.
  5. Bacon back on top, broken into pieces. Black pepper. Chili pepper water at the table. Eat it out of the skillet if you want. There is no rice to plate around.

Kitchen-Estimate Macros (per serving)

Kitchen estimates only, not lab-tested. Calculated for 1 of 2 servings (3 slices bacon, 2 eggs, half the bunch). Watercress volume varies with how hard you wilt it.

Notes

  • Hidden sugar / starch: the diner version is the rice. Some “local breakfast” plates also drop in gravy. Skip gravy. Sweet chili sauce does not belong here either.
  • Watercress is peppery. If a guest is new to it, tell them before they take a stem-end bite and decide they hate Honolulu greens.
  • Portuguese sausage instead of bacon is fine. Then you are next door to the skillet recipe. I still want the watercress, not cabbage, when the bunch is good.
  • Leftover wilted watercress is limp in the fridge. Cook what you will eat. Bacon and eggs reheat; the greens do not.

— Mark Souza
Honolulu

title: Coconut-Milk Chicken Thighs with Bok Choy, Ginger, and Chili
excerpt: Coconut milk in Honolulu is a pantry can, not a dessert. This is chicken thighs simmered in unsweetened coconut milk with ginger, garlic, and chili, and a pile of bok choy wilted in at the end. It reads like the savory coconut dishes I grew up around — Chinese-Hawaiian home cooking — not Thai takeout […]
html:
Coconut milk in Honolulu is a pantry can, not a dessert. This is chicken thighs simmered in unsweetened coconut milk with ginger, garlic, and chili, and a pile of bok choy wilted in at the end. It reads like the savory coconut dishes I grew up around — Chinese-Hawaiian home cooking — not Thai takeout and not haupia. No pineapple. No sweet chili sauce. No “tropical.”

Yield: 4 servings  |  Prep: 15 minutes  |  Cook: 35 minutes  |  Total: about 50 minutes

Hawaii Grocery Notes

  • Costco: boneless skinless chicken thighs. Sometimes boxed unsweetened coconut milk; check the label for sugar. Butter, garlic.
  • Foodland / Times: canned full-fat unsweetened coconut milk (Aroy-D or similar — ingredients should be coconut and water). Fresh ginger, garlic, Hawaiian chili peppers or a red chili, green onion.
  • Don Quijote: bok choy or baby bok choy, ginger, chili, more coconut milk brands. Walk past the sweet coconut drinks and the coconut jelly cups.
  • Lite coconut milk is mostly water. Get the regular can and stir the fat back in. If the ingredient list has sugar, put it back.

Ingredients

  • 1½ lb boneless skinless chicken thighs, patted dry, cut into large chunks
  • 1 tablespoon avocado oil or coconut oil
  • 1 (13.5 oz) can full-fat unsweetened coconut milk, well stirred
  • 1 tablespoon grated fresh ginger
  • 4 garlic cloves, minced
  • 2–4 Hawaiian chili peppers, sliced, or 1 small red chili (seeds in if you want it hot)
  • 1 tablespoon shoyu
  • ½ teaspoon kosher salt, plus more to taste
  • Black pepper
  • 1 lb bok choy or baby bok choy, halved or chopped, washed well
  • 2 green onions, sliced
  • Optional: squeeze of lime at the table (not in the pot — lime juice cooked in coconut milk can go bitter)

Instructions

  1. Season the chicken with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a wide pot or deep skillet over medium-high. Brown the thighs in a single layer, 3–4 minutes a side, until they take color. Do two batches if you have to. They do not need to cook through yet.
  2. Drop the heat to medium. Add ginger, garlic, and chili to the fat in the pan. Stir 30–45 seconds until it smells like dinner, not until the garlic browns.
  3. Pour in the coconut milk and shoyu. Scrape the browned bits. Return all the chicken and any juices. The liquid should come most of the way up the pieces; add a splash of water only if the can was skimpy.
  4. Simmer uncovered 18–22 minutes, turning once, until the chicken is cooked through and the sauce has thickened to a spoon-coating gravy. If it is still thin, simmer a few minutes more. Do not add flour. Do not add cornstarch.
  5. Push the chicken to the sides. Add the bok choy. Cover 3–4 minutes until the stems are tender-crisp and the leaves wilt. Taste the sauce. Add salt if it needs it. It should be savory and a little spicy, not sweet.
  6. Green onions on top. Lime at the table if you want it. Serve in a bowl with plenty of sauce. This is the rice replacement: the sauce and the greens.

Kitchen-Estimate Macros (per serving)

Kitchen estimates only, not lab-tested. Calculated for 1 of 4 servings (chicken, a share of the coconut sauce, and bok choy). Coconut milk brands vary; I used a typical unsweetened full-fat can.

Notes

  • Hidden sugar: sweet chili sauce, bottled “coconut curry” simmer sauces, and some coconut milks. Fish sauce is fine if the bottle is fish and salt; many blends sneak sugar. I use shoyu here because it is what I already have.
  • This is not a Thai curry. No curry paste, no fish-sauce-and-palm-sugar balance, no basil garnish unless that is actually in your fridge. Ginger, chili, coconut, bok choy.
  • Bone-in thighs work. Add 10 minutes and brown them well. Skin-on is even better if you like the fat; Costco’s big tray is usually skinless, and that is what I wrote the times for.
  • Leftovers keep two days. The sauce sets in the fridge; loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat. Better the next day.
  • Same Costco thighs as the pork-rind katsu. Buy the tray, cook both in a week.

title: Pork-Rind Chicken Katsu (No Panko)
excerpt: Katsu on a mixed plate in Honolulu is a fried cutlet, a mountain of shredded cabbage, and a dark sweet sauce. The problem is the panko and the bottle of Bull-Dog. I still want the crunch and I still want cabbage. I do not want the wheat. Crushed pork rinds and an egg wash get […]
html:
Katsu on a mixed plate in Honolulu is a fried cutlet, a mountain of shredded cabbage, and a dark sweet sauce. The problem is the panko and the bottle of Bull-Dog. I still want the crunch and I still want cabbage. I do not want the wheat. Crushed pork rinds and an egg wash get you a crust that actually fries. The sauce is tomato paste, shoyu, Worcestershire, and vinegar — thinner and less sweet than Zippy’s. That is on purpose.

This is not “keto chicken tenders.” It is a cutlet on cabbage with chili pepper water, the way I eat a mixed plate at home.

Yield: 4 servings  |  Prep: 20 minutes  |  Cook: 20 minutes  |  Total: about 40 minutes

Hawaii Grocery Notes

  • Costco: boneless skinless chicken thighs (the big tray). Pork rinds when 4505 is in stock — grab two bags. Avocado oil. Eggs.
  • Foodland / Times: cabbage (cheap, always), tomato paste, Worcestershire, shoyu, rice vinegar, garlic. Hawaiian chili peppers when you see them.
  • Don Quijote: panko aisle you walk past. Shoyu, Worcestershire, chili peppers, cabbage. Kewpie if you want a little on the cabbage, not in the crust.
  • Skip bottled tonkatsu sauce (Bull-Dog and the store brands). Sugar is the first or second ingredient. Skip sweet chili sauce on the side too.

Ingredients

Cutlets

  • 1½ lb boneless skinless chicken thighs (about 6–8 thighs)
  • 2 oz pork rinds (about 2 cups once crushed)
  • 2 large eggs
  • ½ teaspoon kosher salt
  • ½ teaspoon garlic powder
  • Black pepper
  • Avocado oil or tallow, enough for a shallow fry (about ½ cup in a 10-inch skillet)

Sauce (not Bull-Dog)

  • 2 tablespoons tomato paste
  • 1 tablespoon Worcestershire sauce
  • 1 tablespoon shoyu
  • 1 tablespoon rice vinegar or apple cider vinegar
  • 2 tablespoons water
  • Optional: ½ teaspoon monk fruit or allulose if you miss the Zippy’s sweetness. I usually skip it.

Plate

  • ½ small head green cabbage, shredded fine
  • Chili pepper water: 4–6 Hawaiian chili peppers (or 1 small red chili), 1 clove garlic, ½ cup white vinegar, pinch of salt
  • Lemon wedges, optional

Instructions

  1. Crush the pork rinds. A zip bag and a rolling pin, or a few pulses in a processor. You want crumbs the size of coarse panko, not powder. Powder turns gummy.
  2. Pat the thighs dry. If a thigh is very thick, butterfly it so it cooks through before the crust burns. Season both sides with salt, garlic powder, and pepper.
  3. Beat the eggs in a shallow bowl. Put the pork-rind crumbs in another. Dip each thigh in egg, then crumbs, pressing so the crust sticks. Set them on a plate. If the crust looks thin, a second dip is fine.
  4. Make the sauce: stir tomato paste, Worcestershire, shoyu, vinegar, and water in a small saucepan over low heat until it loosens, 2–3 minutes. Taste. Add the optional sweetener only if you want it. Keep it pourable, not sticky-sweet.
  5. Chili pepper water, if you do not already have a jar: smash the peppers and garlic with salt, cover with vinegar, and let it sit while you fry. It is ready enough for the table today and better tomorrow.
  6. Heat a generous film of oil in a skillet over medium. It should shimmer, not smoke. Fry the cutlets 3–5 minutes per side until the crust is deep gold and the chicken is cooked through. Do not crowd the pan. Drain on a rack or paper towels.
  7. Slice the katsu. Pile the cabbage. Spoon a little sauce on the meat, not a puddle on the cabbage. Chili pepper water on the side. Eat it like a mixed plate, not like tenders with ranch.

Kitchen-Estimate Macros (per serving)

Kitchen estimates only, not lab-tested. Calculated for 1 of 4 servings (about 6 oz chicken plus crust and 1–2 tablespoons sauce). Cabbage is extra, roughly 2 g net per cup shredded. Oil absorption varies with how hot your pan is.

Notes

  • Hidden sugar / starch: panko is wheat. Bull-Dog and most “katsu sauces” are sugar first. Furikake on the cabbage is often sugary too — read the label or skip it. Restaurant katsu is a mixed-plate protein sitting next to two scoops of rice; the rice is the other problem.
  • Pork rinds at Costco (4505) disappear for weeks. If the bag is gone, almond flour is a backup crust, but it browns faster and tastes like almond flour. I would rather wait for rinds.
  • Bake at 425°F on a rack for 18–22 minutes if you do not want to fry. The crust is drier. Still better than no katsu.
  • Leftover slices are good cold the next day, or reheated in a skillet so the crust comes back. Microwave turns them sad.
  • This is the protein I swap onto a weeknight mixed plate when I am tired of rotisserie chicken.

title: Weeknight Mixed Plate: Rotisserie + Kalua Leftovers + Chili-Cabbage Slaw
excerpt: A mixed plate in Honolulu is two proteins, two sides, and a mountain of rice. I still want the two proteins and a crunchy side. I do not want the rice or the mac salad that tastes like sugar once you start reading labels. This is my weeknight version: Costco rotisserie chicken, leftover kalua pig […]
html:
A mixed plate in Honolulu is two proteins, two sides, and a mountain of rice. I still want the two proteins and a crunchy side. I do not want the rice or the mac salad that tastes like sugar once you start reading labels. This is my weeknight version: Costco rotisserie chicken, leftover kalua pig from the slow cooker, and a chili-cabbage slaw that takes ten minutes. It is not a new recipe so much as how I actually eat when the week is already in motion.

Yield: 4 plates  |  Prep: 15 minutes  |  Cook: 10 minutes (to reheat)  |  Total: about 25 minutes, if the kalua is already done

Hawaii Grocery Notes

  • Costco: rotisserie chicken at the door. I pull meat off while it is still warm and store it in a container so I am not carving at 6 p.m. Also a second cabbage if the kalua pot used the first one.
  • Foodland / Times: cabbage, green onion, chili pepper water, mayo, a lime or lemon.
  • Don Quijote: chili garlic sauce, rice vinegar, sesame oil, extra mayo.
  • Rotisserie chicken is convenient. Some birds are injected. Costco’s is the one I use; still, if a store bird tastes sweet, I do not buy that store’s chicken again.

Ingredients

Proteins

  • 1 Costco (or similar) rotisserie chicken, meat pulled — you will use about 1 lb meat for 4 plates (save the rest for eggs tomorrow)
  • 2–3 cups leftover kalua pig, with some cabbage if you have it
  • 2 tablespoons of the kalua juices or butter, for reheating

Chili-cabbage slaw

  • 6 cups finely shredded green cabbage (about ½ large head)
  • 2 green onions, sliced
  • ⅓ cup mayonnaise
  • 1 tablespoon rice vinegar or lemon juice
  • 1–2 teaspoons chili garlic sauce or homemade chili pepper water, to taste
  • 1 teaspoon toasted sesame oil (optional)
  • Pinch of salt and black pepper
  • Optional: 1 tablespoon chopped cilantro if you like it

Plate

  • Lemon wedges
  • Extra chili pepper water at the table

Instructions

  1. Stir the slaw dressing: mayo, vinegar, chili sauce or chili pepper water, sesame oil, salt, pepper. Taste. It should be sharp and a little spicy, not sweet. If it tastes like restaurant mac salad, you added the wrong sauce.
  2. Toss cabbage and green onion with the dressing. Set aside 10 minutes so the cabbage softens slightly. It should still crunch.
  3. Reheat kalua pig in a skillet with a spoon of its juices or a little butter, just until hot. Do not boil it dry.
  4. Pull or slice the rotisserie chicken. Dark meat is the better mixed-plate energy. Warm it in the same pan for a minute if it is fridge-cold, or serve it room temp. I do not microwave it if I can help it.
  5. Build plates: a scoop of kalua, a scoop of chicken, a pile of slaw. Lemon over the chicken. Chili pepper water on everything. That is a mixed plate. Sit down and eat it while it is hot.

Kitchen-Estimate Macros (per serving)

Kitchen estimates only, not lab-tested. Calculated for 4 oz rotisserie meat (mostly thigh), 3 oz kalua pig, and about 1½ cups dressed slaw. Using more skin-on dark meat raises fat; using only breast lowers it. Chili sauces with sugar will move net carbs.

Notes

  • Hidden sugar: store mac salad, bottled “island” dressings, teriyaki drizzle, and sweet chili sauce will turn this into a regular mixed plate with a keto costume. Mayo + vinegar + chili pepper water is the slaw. Read the rotisserie ingredient list once so you know what you are buying.
  • No kalua leftovers? Two rotisserie chickens and extra slaw still works. Or swap Kahuku-style garlic shrimp as the second protein.
  • This is the leftover strategy in practice: Sunday or Monday kalua pig is not one dinner. It is this plate, a breakfast skillet, and maybe a wrap in lettuce on Thursday.
  • Pack the slaw separate if this is lunch. Dressed cabbage weeps. Still edible. Less crisp.

title: Pan-Seared Ahi with Ginger-Garlic Butter
excerpt: Fresh ahi is one of the actual luxuries of cooking in Honolulu, and it is wasted under a sweet glaze. I sear steaks hot and fast and spoon ginger-garlic butter over the top while they rest. Twenty minutes, one pan, and it tastes like I tried. This is early dinner on a work night when […]
html:
Fresh ahi is one of the actual luxuries of cooking in Honolulu, and it is wasted under a sweet glaze. I sear steaks hot and fast and spoon ginger-garlic butter over the top while they rest. Twenty minutes, one pan, and it tastes like I tried. This is early dinner on a work night when I already used my energy at Costco, not on a recipe with twelve steps.

Yield: 4 servings  |  Prep: 10 minutes  |  Cook: 8 minutes  |  Total: about 20 minutes

Hawaii Grocery Notes

  • Foodland / Times: ahi steaks, 1 to 1½ inches thick if you can get them. Thicker is more forgiving. Ask for sushi-grade if you want the center rare, which I do.
  • Costco: frozen ahi steaks in the freezer aisle when fresh is a splurge. Thaw overnight in the fridge. Pat extra dry.
  • Don Quijote: fresh ginger, garlic, butter, sesame oil, shoyu, chili flakes.
  • Skip bottled teriyaki, eel sauce, and “Hawaiian” glazes. None of them belong on this fish.

Ingredients

  • 4 ahi steaks (about 6 oz each), 1–1½ inches thick, patted dry
  • 1 tablespoon avocado oil
  • Kosher salt and black pepper
  • 5 tablespoons unsalted butter
  • 3 garlic cloves, minced
  • 1 tablespoon fresh ginger, minced or grated
  • 1 teaspoon shoyu or tamari
  • 1 teaspoon lemon juice or rice vinegar
  • Optional: pinch of chili flakes
  • Optional: 1 teaspoon toasted sesame seeds
  • For the plate: a pile of greens, steamed broccoli, or leftover cabbage from kalua pig

Instructions

  1. Salt and pepper both sides of the ahi. Let it sit at room temperature 10 minutes while you mince garlic and ginger. Cold, wet fish will not sear.
  2. Heat a skillet over high until it is very hot. Add avocado oil. It should shimmer.
  3. Lay in the steaks. Do not move them. Sear 60–90 seconds per side for rare to mid-rare on a 1-inch steak. Thicker steaks can go 2 minutes per side. You want a browned crust and a deep pink center. If you cook ahi like chicken, you will be mad at me and at the fish.
  4. Transfer steaks to a warm plate. Drop the heat to low. Add butter to the same pan. When it melts, add garlic and ginger. Stir 30–45 seconds until fragrant, not brown.
  5. Add shoyu, lemon juice, and chili flakes. Stir once. Spoon the butter over the steaks. Rest 2 minutes. Sesame seeds on top if you are using them.
  6. Serve with greens or leftover cabbage. Spoon extra butter from the plate. That butter is dinner, not a garnish.

Kitchen-Estimate Macros (per serving)

Kitchen estimates only, not lab-tested. Calculated for one 6 oz steak plus a quarter of the ginger-garlic butter. Side vegetables not included (broccoli ~4 g net per cup; wilted greens ~1–2 g).

Notes

  • Hidden sugar: ponzu, teriyaki, oyster sauce, and bottled ginger dressings often carry sugar or mirin. The teaspoon of shoyu in this pan is there for salt and color. If even that bothers you, drop it and add a pinch more salt.
  • Sesame-crusted ahi is fine on keto. Press seeds onto the raw steak before the sear. Count a gram or two extra if you go heavy.
  • Leftover seared ahi is better cold, sliced over greens, than reheated. Reheating is how you get dry fish.

title: Portuguese Sausage Breakfast Skillet
excerpt: Portuguese sausage and eggs is a Honolulu breakfast I ate long before I ate keto. The usual plate is sausage, eggs, and two scoops of rice. I kept the sausage and the eggs and gave the rice job to cabbage, which fries in the rendered fat and actually tastes like it belongs there. This is […]
html:
Portuguese sausage and eggs is a Honolulu breakfast I ate long before I ate keto. The usual plate is sausage, eggs, and two scoops of rice. I kept the sausage and the eggs and gave the rice job to cabbage, which fries in the rendered fat and actually tastes like it belongs there. This is late breakfast for me — the meal that opens the eating window — and it is also dinner on nights I do not want to think.

Yield: 4 servings  |  Prep: 10 minutes  |  Cook: 20 minutes  |  Total: about 30 minutes

Hawaii Grocery Notes

  • Foodland / Times: Redondo’s, Purity, or house Portuguese sausage in the meat case. Turn the package over. If sugar is high on the ingredient list or carbs are more than a couple grams per serving, pick another pack or use less sausage and more eggs.
  • Don Quijote: several island sausage brands, plus cabbage, onions, eggs, chili pepper water.
  • Costco: eggs, butter, a whole cabbage. Portuguese sausage is hit-or-miss there; I usually get it at Foodland.
  • This is not linguica from the mainland catalog, and it is not SPAM with “Portuguese sausage seasoning” unless that is honestly all you can find. Real island Portuguese sausage is the point.

Ingredients

  • 12 oz Portuguese sausage, sliced into ¼-inch coins
  • 8 large eggs
  • ½ small yellow onion, thinly sliced (keep it modest — onion is the carb you can see)
  • 4 cups shredded green cabbage (about ½ small head)
  • 1 tablespoon butter, if the sausage does not render enough fat
  • Black pepper
  • Pinch of paprika or chili flakes
  • Optional: 2 oz leftover kalua pig, chopped, if you have it
  • Optional: chili pepper water or hot sauce with no sugar on the label
  • Optional: sliced avocado on the side
  • Salt only after tasting — sausage is already salty

Instructions

  1. Set a 12-inch skillet (cast iron if you have it) over medium heat. Add the sausage coins in a single layer. Cook until both sides are browned and some fat has rendered, 6–8 minutes. Transfer sausage to a plate. Leave the fat in the pan.
  2. If the pan looks dry, add the butter. Add onion and cook 2 minutes until it just starts to soften.
  3. Add cabbage and a few grinds of pepper. Toss in the fat until the cabbage wilts and takes on color, 5–7 minutes. You want fried cabbage, not steamed cabbage. If it is crowding, give it another minute rather than adding water.
  4. Stir the sausage (and kalua, if using) back in. Taste. Add salt only if it needs it. Paprika or chili flakes now.
  5. Make four wells in the cabbage. Crack an egg into each well, or beat all eight eggs and pour them over for a scramble. I do whole eggs in wells when I have the extra two minutes; scramble when I am in a hurry.
  6. Cover and cook until the whites are set and yolks are how you like them, 3–5 minutes. For scrambled, stir gently until just set.
  7. Serve from the skillet. Chili pepper water on top. Avocado on the side if you want more fat and a softer plate.

Kitchen-Estimate Macros (per serving)

Kitchen estimates only, not lab-tested. Assumes 3 oz sausage, 2 eggs, and cabbage, using a typical island Portuguese sausage around 2–3 g carbohydrate per serving. Read your label; some brands run higher because of added sugar. Avocado not included (~2 g net per half).

Notes

  • Hidden sugar: Portuguese sausage is the label you actually have to read in Hawaii. Many recipes treat it as zero-carb. It is not always. If your brand is sweet, brown less of it and fill the pan with eggs and cabbage, or switch brands next shop.
  • Leftover kalua pig in this skillet is one of the better breakfasts in my house. Sausage plus kalua is a lot of salt — taste before you add any.
  • This reheats. The eggs do not get better in the microwave, but the sausage-cabbage mix is fine the next day with a fresh fried egg on top.

title: SPAM Musubi Without Rice
excerpt: Musubi is convenience food in Honolulu. It is also rice wrapped in nori with a slice of SPAM, which does not fit how I eat. I still want the shape, the nori, and that salty-crisp SPAM edge, so I swapped the rice for a thin egg slab that holds together in the mold. It tastes […]
html:
Musubi is convenience food in Honolulu. It is also rice wrapped in nori with a slice of SPAM, which does not fit how I eat. I still want the shape, the nori, and that salty-crisp SPAM edge, so I swapped the rice for a thin egg slab that holds together in the mold. It tastes like a musubi, not like a lecture. I make a pan of them, wrap them, and that is lunch at the beach or in the car without hunting for a “keto” cafe.

Yield: 6 musubi (1 as a snack, 2 as a meal)  |  Prep: 15 minutes  |  Cook: 20 minutes  |  Total: about 35 minutes

Hawaii Grocery Notes

  • Costco: SPAM Classic 8-pack. This is the can you want. Do not grab Teriyaki, Hot Honey, or whatever limited flavor is on the endcap.
  • Don Quijote: nori sheets, furikake (read the sugar line), Kewpie, extra Classic if Costco was a zoo.
  • Foodland / Times: eggs, butter, Classic singles if you only need one can.
  • SPAM Classic still has a gram of sugar per 2 oz serving from the formula. That is not the same as Teriyaki SPAM, which is a different product with a sweet glaze built in.

Ingredients

  • 1 can (12 oz) SPAM Classic, sliced into 6 even slabs
  • 6 large eggs
  • 2 tablespoons water or unsweetened almond milk
  • 1 tablespoon butter, plus more for the pan
  • 6 full nori sheets, or 6 half-sheets if you like less wrap
  • Black pepper
  • Optional: 1 teaspoon shoyu in the eggs (adds a little carb; skip if you are tight that day)
  • Optional: unsweetened furikake or toasted sesame seeds and salt (many furikake blends add sugar — flip the bottle)
  • Optional crunch layer: ½ cup crushed pork rinds, divided

Instructions

  1. Beat the eggs with water, pepper, and the shoyu if using. You want a thin omelet batter, not scrambled-egg chunks.
  2. Heat a nonstick skillet over medium. Melt a little butter. Pour in one-sixth of the eggs and tilt into a rectangle roughly the size of a musubi mold (about 3½ × 2 inches is ideal; a slightly larger thin sheet you can trim is fine). Cook until just set. Flip if you need to. Stack the six egg slabs on a plate. They should be pliable, not browned hard.
  3. Wipe the pan. Fry the SPAM slabs over medium heat until both sides are well browned and the edges crisp, 2–3 minutes per side. Do not add sugar, honey, or teriyaki to the pan. The can already has salt. Drain on paper towel.
  4. If you have a musubi mold, set it on a nori sheet (shiny side down). If not, use wet hands and pack tightly; a both-ends-open can works as a mold.
  5. Layer: egg slab, optional sprinkle of crushed pork rinds, SPAM, optional sesame or unsweetened furikake. Press firmly so it holds. Wrap the nori around and seal the edge with a dab of water.
  6. Rest 2 minutes so the nori softens and sticks. Slice in half if you want, or eat it like a local gas-station musubi, in the parking lot, with a napkin.

Kitchen-Estimate Macros

Kitchen estimates only, not lab-tested. SPAM Classic, not Teriyaki. Pork rinds optional and not included below.

Notes

  • Hidden sugar: SPAM Teriyaki, Lite (sometimes odd fillers), and most musubi-stand glazes are the problem. Classic only. Skip the pan glaze of sugar-shoyu that every viral recipe uses. Furikake is a second trap — nori komi without sugar, or sesame and salt.
  • Cauliflower rice musubi is a thing. I have made it. It is wet unless you cook the cauli dry and bind it with a little cream cheese. The egg slab is more reliable in a Honolulu kitchen with no special gear.
  • These keep, wrapped, in the fridge a day. Nori softens. That is normal. Recrisp the SPAM side in a dry pan if you care.

title: Spicy Ahi on Won Bok (Not a Rice Bowl)
excerpt: I like poke as much as anyone who lives here. I do not like pretending a sweet, sticky bowl with a scoop of rice is “keto because ahi.” This is spicy ahi the way I actually eat it at home: sushi-grade fish, a sauce I mix myself, and a bed of won bok instead of […]
html:
I like poke as much as anyone who lives here. I do not like pretending a sweet, sticky bowl with a scoop of rice is “keto because ahi.” This is spicy ahi the way I actually eat it at home: sushi-grade fish, a sauce I mix myself, and a bed of won bok instead of rice. Won bok is napa cabbage. It is cheap, it is at Foodland and Times every week, and it gives you something to push the ahi around with.

Yield: 4 servings  |  Prep: 20 minutes  |  Cook: 5 minutes (won bok only)  |  Total: about 25 minutes

Hawaii Grocery Notes

  • Foodland / Times: poke-grade or sashimi-grade ahi. Buy plain cubes or a steak you cube at home. Walk past the pre-mixed spicy poke if the label lists sugar, mirin, or “poke sauce.”
  • Costco: frozen ahi steaks when the fresh case is expensive. Thaw in the fridge. Won bok / napa is often in the produce bins too.
  • Don Quijote: Kewpie mayo, toasted sesame oil, roasted sesame seeds, chili garlic sauce, nori komi (check sugar), green onion, shoyu.
  • Won bok is the pale, crinkly napa cabbage, not round green cabbage. Either works. Won bok is softer and more “bowl-like.”

Ingredients

Ahi

  • 1 lb sushi-grade ahi, cut into ½-inch cubes, very cold
  • 2 green onions, thinly sliced
  • 1 teaspoon toasted sesame seeds
  • 1 sheet nori, torn or snipped into thin strips (optional)

Homemade spicy sauce (mix in a bowl; do not buy bottled poke sauce)

  • ⅓ cup mayonnaise (Best Foods Real for 0 g sugar per tbsp; Kewpie if you like it and will count ~1 g per tbsp)
  • 2 teaspoons chili garlic sauce or sriracha (read the label; many brands add sugar)
  • 1 teaspoon toasted sesame oil
  • 1 teaspoon shoyu or tamari
  • ½ teaspoon rice vinegar or lemon juice
  • Pinch of kosher salt

Won bok bed

  • 1 medium won bok (napa cabbage), about 1½ lb, sliced into wide ribbons
  • 1 tablespoon avocado oil or sesame oil
  • Pinch of salt

Instructions

  1. Keep the ahi in the fridge until the sauce and cabbage are ready. Cold fish cubes better and tastes cleaner.
  2. Stir the sauce until it is smooth. Taste it. You want spicy, salty, and a little tang. If it tastes sweet, your chili sauce has sugar — switch brands or cut it with more mayo and vinegar.
  3. Heat a wide pan over medium-high. Add oil, then the won bok and a pinch of salt. Toss 2–4 minutes until the ribs are just tender and the leaves are wilted but not soggy. You can also keep it raw and sliced thin, like a slaw. I usually wilt it so it eats like a warm bowl.
  4. Divide the won bok into four bowls. Let it sit one minute so it is not piping hot under raw fish.
  5. Toss the cold ahi with the sauce, most of the green onion, and sesame seeds. Do not let it sit in sauce for an hour; 2–5 minutes is plenty.
  6. Spoon the ahi over the won bok. Finish with nori strips and the rest of the green onion. Serve immediately.

Kitchen-Estimate Macros (per serving)

Kitchen estimates only, not lab-tested. Calculated for 1 of 4 servings using Best Foods Real mayo and a chili garlic sauce with little or no added sugar. Kewpie and a sugary sriracha will nudge net carbs up by 1–2 g.

Notes

  • Hidden sugar: bottled poke sauce, store spicy ahi, and several chili sauces are the trap. Mix the sauce at home. Skip teriyaki, unagi sauce, and anything labeled “Hawaiian” that lists pineapple or brown sugar.
  • If you do not eat raw fish, sear the cubes 20–30 seconds in a hot pan and toss with sauce off heat. It is a different dish. Still good. Still not a rice bowl.
  • Leftover sauced ahi is not a meal-prep hero. Mix what you will eat. Extra plain cubes keep a day, well chilled.
  • A drizzle of homemade chili pepper water on the won bok is very Hawaii and usually just chili, vinegar, garlic, and salt — check that nobody added sugar to the bottle.

title: Kahuku-Style Garlic Shrimp (No Flour)
excerpt: The North Shore shrimp trucks are a Honolulu ritual, and they dredge. Flour is how Giovanni’s and the rest get that crust and that clingy garlic butter. I want the same pile of shrimp and the same ridiculous amount of garlic without the flour, so this is a hard sear in a hot pan and […]
html:
The North Shore shrimp trucks are a Honolulu ritual, and they dredge. Flour is how Giovanni’s and the rest get that crust and that clingy garlic butter. I want the same pile of shrimp and the same ridiculous amount of garlic without the flour, so this is a hard sear in a hot pan and a whole head of garlic in butter. It is a weeknight dish. It is also what I cook when someone is visiting and thinks keto in Hawaii means sad salad.

Yield: 4 servings  |  Prep: 15 minutes  |  Cook: 12 minutes  |  Total: about 25 minutes

Hawaii Grocery Notes

  • Costco: 2 lb frozen shrimp (16–20 or 21–25 count), tail on. Thaw in the fridge overnight or under cold water. Also butter in the big pack.
  • Foodland / Times: fresh garlic (buy extra), lemons, parsley if you want it, a head of won bok or a bag of salad greens for the plate.
  • Don Quijote: garlic by the bag, butter, chili pepper flakes, Kewpie if you want a little on the side (not in the pan).
  • Do not buy pre-sauced “garlic shrimp” from a hot case. That sauce is usually sweet and often thickened with starch.

Ingredients

  • 1½ lb large shrimp, peeled, tail on, patted very dry
  • 8 tablespoons unsalted butter (1 stick), divided
  • 1 tablespoon avocado oil or tallow
  • 1 large head garlic (10–14 cloves), peeled and roughly chopped — this is supposed to look like too much garlic
  • ½ teaspoon paprika
  • ¼ teaspoon cayenne, or to taste
  • ¾ teaspoon kosher salt, plus more at the table
  • Black pepper
  • 1 tablespoon lemon juice
  • Optional: pinch of xanthan gum (literally 1/16 teaspoon) if you want the butter slightly clingy
  • Optional: chopped parsley or green onion
  • For the plate: steamed or pan-wilted won bok, or a simple green salad with olive oil

Instructions

  1. Thaw and peel the shrimp if needed. Leave the tails on; they help you flip and they look like the truck plate. Pat until the paper towel comes away dry. Wet shrimp will steam and you will lose the sear.
  2. Season the shrimp with salt, pepper, paprika, and cayenne. No flour. No cornstarch. No “light dusting.”
  3. Heat a wide skillet over medium-high until it is properly hot. Add the oil and 2 tablespoons of the butter.
  4. Add shrimp in a single layer. Do two batches if you have to. Cook 1½–2 minutes per side until just opaque and browned in spots. Transfer to a plate. They will finish in the butter.
  5. Drop the heat to medium-low. Add the remaining 6 tablespoons butter and the chopped garlic. Stir 1–2 minutes until the garlic is fragrant and just turning gold at the edges. If it starts to brown hard, pull the pan off the heat. Burnt garlic is bitter and it will wreck the batch.
  6. Return the shrimp and any plate juices. Toss 30–45 seconds. Add lemon juice. If you are using the pinch of xanthan, sprinkle it over the butter while tossing so it does not clump.
  7. Taste the butter. Add salt if it needs it. Serve immediately over won bok or greens, with extra garlic spooned on top. Eat the garlic. That is the point.

Kitchen-Estimate Macros (per serving)

Kitchen estimates only, not lab-tested. Calculated for 1 of 4 servings (about 6 oz shrimp plus garlic butter). Won bok on the side is extra, roughly 2 g net per cup cooked.

Notes

  • Hidden sugar / starch: the truck version is floured, and many copycat recipes add sugar to the butter. Skip both. Paprika and lemon do the work. Bottled garlic-butter sauces are usually sweet; make it in the pan.
  • Garlic is a carb. A whole head split four ways still lands this plate under about 10 g net. Do not “keto it” by cutting the garlic in half. Then it is just shrimp in butter.
  • Heads-on shrimp from a shrimp shack are a different cook. This recipe is for the peeled tails you can actually buy on a Tuesday at Costco.
  • Leftover shrimp are decent cold the next day, but garlic butter firms up in the fridge. Reheat gently; do not microwave them into rubber.

title: Slow-Cooker Kalua Pig with Cabbage
excerpt: I do not have an imu in the backyard. I have a slow cooker, a Costco pork shoulder, Hawaiian salt, and a bottle of liquid smoke, and that is how kalua pig happens on a regular week in Honolulu. This is the pot I start in the morning when I want dinner to take care […]
html:
I do not have an imu in the backyard. I have a slow cooker, a Costco pork shoulder, Hawaiian salt, and a bottle of liquid smoke, and that is how kalua pig happens on a regular week in Honolulu. This is the pot I start in the morning when I want dinner to take care of itself, and it is the pot that feeds me again two or three days later. The cabbage is not a garnish. It sits in the drippings at the end and becomes the “starch” of the plate.

Yield: 8 servings  |  Prep: 15 minutes  |  Cook: 8–10 hours on low  |  Total: about 8½–10½ hours (mostly unattended)

Hawaii Grocery Notes

  • Costco (Iwilei, Hawaii Kai, Kapolei): boneless pork shoulder / pork butt, usually 4–7 lb. One pack is a week of protein. Also grab a big green cabbage if the price is better than Foodland that day.
  • Foodland / Times: alaea (red Hawaiian) salt in the spice aisle; green cabbage; banana leaf if you want the aroma and they have it (optional, not required).
  • Don Quijote: liquid smoke if Costco is out; extra cabbage; Hawaiian salt.
  • Skip bottled “kalua seasoning kits” that hide sugar. Salt, smoke, pork, cabbage. That is the list.

Ingredients

  • 4½–5 lb boneless pork shoulder (pork butt), skin off, excess hard fat trimmed but leave the good fat
  • 1 tablespoon alaea Hawaiian salt (or coarse sea salt), plus more to taste after shredding
  • 1½ teaspoons liquid smoke (hickory or mesquite)
  • ½ cup water
  • 1 large green cabbage (about 2–2½ lb), cored and cut into thick wedges
  • Optional: 2 tablespoons bacon drippings or lard if your shoulder looks very lean
  • Optional: banana leaf to line the cooker, well rinsed

Instructions

  1. Pat the pork dry. Rub the Hawaiian salt over all sides. If you have time, salt it the night before and refrigerate uncovered; if not, salt it and go.
  2. If using banana leaf, line the slow cooker. Set the pork in, fat-cap up. Sprinkle the liquid smoke over the meat. Add the water around the sides, not on top of the salt crust. Add bacon drippings if the shoulder is lean.
  3. Cook on low 8–10 hours, until the pork pulls apart with two forks. A 5 lb shoulder is usually right at 9 hours in my cooker.
  4. Lift the pork onto a board. Pour the cooking juices into a fat separator or a bowl and skim. You want the juices; you do not want a cup of pure fat on the cabbage.
  5. Return ½–¾ cup of the juices to the cooker. Add the cabbage wedges. Cover and cook on high 35–50 minutes, until the cabbage is tender and stained with drippings but not collapsed into soup.
  6. Shred the pork with two forks. Toss with a splash of reserved juices and a pinch more salt if it needs it. Kalua pig should taste like salt and smoke, not like barbecue sauce.
  7. Serve a heap of pork over a cabbage wedge. That is the plate. No rice, no mac salad, no sweet glaze.
  8. Cool leftovers in shallow containers. Refrigerate up to 4 days or freeze in meal-size bags. This pot is how the weeknight mixed plate happens later.

Kitchen-Estimate Macros (per serving)

Kitchen estimates only, not lab-tested. Calculated for 1 of 8 servings (about 5–6 oz cooked pork plus cabbage). Your shoulder’s fat cap and how much juice you add back will move these numbers.

Notes

  • Hidden sugar: stay away from bottled kalua or “Hawaiian barbecue” sauces, and do not finish this with teriyaki. The smoke and salt are the seasoning.
  • Instant Pot version if you are home at lunch: 90 minutes high pressure on a 4½–5 lb shoulder, natural release 20 minutes, then sauté the cabbage in the juices.
  • Too smoky is easy. Start with 1½ teaspoons. You can add a few drops after shredding; you cannot take it out.
  • The cabbage is doing the job rice used to do on a local plate: soaking up juice and making the serving feel complete.
  • This recipe is the leftover engine of my week. Plan on it showing up in the mixed plate and in a breakfast skillet with eggs.

title: The Dirty Keto Diet Explained
excerpt: Dirty Keto is a variation of the traditional Ketogenic (Keto) diet that places a primary focus on macronutrient composition while paying less attention to the quality of food sources.
html:
Dirty Keto is a variation of the traditional Ketogenic (Keto) diet that places a primary focus on macronutrient composition while paying less attention to the quality of food sources. In a standard Keto diet, the goal is to achieve a state of ketosis, where your body primarily burns fat for energy by drastically reducing carbohydrate intake and increasing fat intake. However, in Dirty Keto, the emphasis is primarily on the macronutrient ratios (high fat, low carbs, moderate protein) without much regard for the nutritional quality of the foods consumed.

Here are key characteristics of Dirty Keto:

  1. High Fat, Low Carbs: Like the classic Keto diet, Dirty Keto is characterized by a high intake of healthy fats, typically comprising 70-80% of daily calories. Carbohydrate intake is severely restricted, usually to less than 50 grams of net carbs per day, and sometimes even lower.
  2. Low Carbohydrate Intake: The primary goal is to keep carbohydrate consumption minimal to maintain ketosis, a metabolic state where the body relies on fat for fuel instead of carbohydrates.
  3. Moderate Protein: Protein intake on Dirty Keto is typically moderate, making up around 15-20% of daily calories. This helps prevent excess protein from converting into glucose, which could hinder ketosis.

However, the “dirty” aspect of Dirty Keto refers to the fact that it allows for the consumption of processed and less nutritious food choices as long as they fit the macronutrient criteria. This can include foods like fast food burgers without buns, processed meats, artificial sweeteners, and low-carb packaged snacks. While this version of the keto diet can be considered much for convenient and “fun” than the standard keto diet, processed foods (especially those containing added sugars and seed oils) can eliminate the long term benefits of following a keto diet lifestyle.

Here are some important points to consider about Dirty Keto:

  • Nutrient Deficiency: One of the primary concerns with Dirty Keto is the potential for nutrient deficiencies. By prioritizing macronutrient ratios while neglecting the quality of food sources, individuals on this diet may miss out on essential vitamins, minerals, and other micronutrients. Fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, which are rich in these nutrients, are often limited or excluded from the diet. Over time, this can lead to deficiencies in vitamins such as vitamin C, vitamin K and minerals like potassium, magnesium, and fiber.
  • Gut Health: A diet low in fiber from vegetables and fruits can negatively impact gut health. Fiber is essential for maintaining a healthy gut microbiome and supporting regular bowel movements. Without an adequate intake of fiber, individuals may experience digestive issues such as constipation, bloating, and a higher risk of gastrointestinal problems.
  • Cardiovascular Health: While Dirty Keto may help some individuals lose weight initially, it can raise concerns about long-term cardiovascular health. The diet often relies on high saturated fat sources, including processed meats and artificial trans fats found in some low-carb packaged foods. A diet high in these types of fats may increase the risk of heart disease and other cardiovascular problems.
  • Inflammatory Response: The lack of anti-inflammatory foods, such as colorful vegetables and fruits, and the higher concentration of seed oils in Dirty Keto can contribute to chronic inflammation. Inflammation is associated with various health issues, including autoimmune diseases, arthritis, and an increased risk of chronic diseases.

It’s important to note that individual responses to diets vary, and some people may experience success with Dirty Keto in the short term. However, it’s crucial to consider the potential long-term risks and to consult with a nutritionist or registered dietitian before embarking on any diet plan. They can help you make informed choices that align with your health goals while minimizing the negative health risks associated with diets like Dirty Keto.

Like many things in life, dirty keto is best done in moderation and not as your full time lifestyle. If a social situation arises, such as a company or family party, or some other outside event where you don’t control the menu, the dirty keto diet can be useful. Otherwise, follow the sustainable whole foods practices of the standard keto diet to live your best life!

title: Carnivore Diet vs Keto – Which is the Best Lifestyle for Optimal Health
excerpt: In the evolving world of dietary trends, the “Carnivore Diet vs Keto” debate has garnered significant attention. Both diets have risen in popularity, each promising unique health benefits and lifestyle transformations. In this article we’ll delve into a comprehensive comparison of these two diets, examining their principles, health impacts, and overall sustainability. Whether you’re considering […]
html:
In the evolving world of dietary trends, the “Carnivore Diet vs Keto” debate has garnered significant attention. Both diets have risen in popularity, each promising unique health benefits and lifestyle transformations. In this article we’ll delve into a comprehensive comparison of these two diets, examining their principles, health impacts, and overall sustainability.

Whether you’re considering a major dietary change or simply curious about these nutritional approaches, this article will provide valuable insights to help guide your decision. Join us as we explore the key differences and similarities between the Carnivore Diet and the Keto Diet, offering an informed perspective on each.

Table of Contents

  • Dietary Principles
  • Macronutrient Composition
  • Food Varieties
  • Health Benefits
  • Risks and Considerations
  • Impact on Physical Performance
  • Scientific Evidence and Studies
  • Cost Comparison
  • Community and Support
  • Personalization and Flexibility
  • Conclusion and Recommendations

Dietary Principles

When comparing the Carnivore Diet and Keto, it’s crucial to understand their core dietary principles. This understanding not only helps in making informed choices but also in effectively implementing these diets to achieve desired health goals.

Carnivore Diet: The Carnivore Diet is straightforward in its approach: consume animal products exclusively, and avoid plant-based foods. This means a diet primarily composed of meat, fish, eggs, and certain dairy products. The focus is on high protein and fat intake, with virtually zero carbohydrates. The simplicity of this diet is one of its key appeals, as it doesn’t require much counting or tracking of macronutrients.

Keto Diet: The Keto Diet, on the other hand, emphasizes drastically reducing carbohydrate intake and replacing it with fat. This shift puts the body in a state of ketosis, where fat, rather than carbohydrates, is burned for energy. Unlike the Carnivore Diet, Keto allows for a broader range of food choices, including meat, fish, eggs, certain dairy products, nuts, seeds, and low-carb vegetables. The key principle is to maintain a specific macronutrient ratio: high fat, moderate protein, and very low carbohydrate.

Comparing Principles: Both diets limit carbohydrate intake, but the Carnivore Diet takes this to an extreme by eliminating them entirely. Keto focuses more on the balance of macronutrients to achieve ketosis. The Carnivore Diet’s simplicity in food choices contrasts with Keto’s slightly more diverse options, which might include keto-friendly desserts or snacks.

Macronutrient Composition

Understanding the macronutrient composition is pivotal in distinguishing the Carnivore Diet from the Keto Diet. Focusing on “Carnivore Diet vs Keto”, we’ll discuss next how each diet allocates fats, proteins, and carbohydrates, the three primary macronutrients in our diet.

Carnivore Diet Macronutrients: The Carnivore Diet is characterized by a high intake of proteins and fats, with an almost non-existent carbohydrate count. Protein sources include meat, fish, and eggs, while fats are obtained from these foods and selected dairy products like cheese and butter. The absence of carbohydrates is a defining feature, making it unique among high-protein diets.

Keto Diet Macronutrients: The Keto Diet, while also low in carbohydrates, has a distinctive macronutrient balance. It requires high fat intake, moderate protein, and very low carbohydrates, typically limiting carbs to 20-50 grams per day. This distribution aims to induce ketosis, a metabolic state where the body utilizes fat for energy instead of carbohydrates. The fat in a Keto Diet comes from sources like avocados, oils, nuts, and fatty meats, while proteins are moderately consumed.

Contrasting the Two: The main difference lies in protein and fat ratios. The Carnivore Diet is heavier in protein, whereas the Keto Diet emphasizes more on fats with controlled protein to maintain ketosis. Both diets are low in carbohydrates, but the Keto Diet includes some, primarily from vegetables and nuts, which are absent in the Carnivore Diet.

Food Varieties

When comparing the “Carnivore Diet vs Keto,” the variety of foods each diet allows is a key differentiator. Now we’ll explore the types of foods that are central to each diet, providing a clear understanding of what you can eat on each.

Carnivore Diet Food Choices: The Carnivore Diet is remarkably straightforward in its food selection: it strictly includes animal products. Key staples are meats of all kinds, including beef (preferable grass-fed and grass-finished), chicken (preferably free range and organic), pork (preferably organic), and fish (preferably wild caught and not farmed). Organ meats like liver and kidney are also encouraged due to their nutrient density. Eggs and certain dairy products, such as cheese and butter, round out the diet’s offerings. There’s no room for fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds, or grains in this diet.

Keto Diet Food Choices: The Keto Diet offers a broader palette. While it also includes meat and dairy (same organic preferences), it integrates a variety of other foods. Essential to the Keto Diet are low-carb vegetables like spinach, kale, and broccoli, which provide necessary nutrients and fiber. Nuts, seeds, and some fruits (mostly berries) are also included. Keto-friendly flours, such as almond and coconut flour, allow for more diverse meal preparations, including baked goods that comply with the diet’s low-carb mandate.

Contrasting the Two: The primary contrast lies in the inclusion of plant-based foods. The Carnivore Diet is exclusive to animal products, whereas the Keto Diet accommodates a more balanced array of food groups, including vegetables, nuts, and limited fruits.

Both lifestyles avoid seed oils as they are high in omega 6 linoleic acid and can cause significant inflammation. Preferably, use beef tallow and avocado oil for high heat cooking, grass fed butter or olive oil for low heat cooking and olive oil for drizzling on meat and salad.

Health Benefits

Exploring the health benefits is a crucial aspect of comparing “Carnivore Diet vs Keto.” Both diets have unique advantages that cater to different health goals and needs.

Carnivore Diet Health Benefits: The Carnivore Diet, with its high intake of animal proteins and fats, offers several health benefits. Proponents of the diet report improved digestive health due to the elimination of plant fibers and carbohydrates. There’s also evidence suggesting benefits in weight loss, reduced inflammation, and enhanced mental clarity. Additionally, the high protein content can be advantageous for muscle building and maintenance.

Keto Diet Health Benefits: The Keto Diet is renowned for its effectiveness in weight loss, primarily due to the state of ketosis, which optimizes fat burning. Beyond weight loss, it’s associated with improved blood sugar control, making it a potential dietary approach for managing diabetes. The diet may also contribute to improved heart health due to the high intake of healthy fats, and some individuals report enhanced mental focus and energy levels.

Comparing the Benefits: While both diets are effective for weight loss and improved metabolic health, the Keto Diet’s inclusion of plant-based foods provides a broader spectrum of nutrients. This can lead to more balanced overall health benefits. In contrast, the Carnivore Diet’s zero-carb approach may be more suitable for those seeking digestive health improvements and a straightforward dietary regimen.

Risks and Considerations

When evaluating “Carnivore Diet vs Keto,” it’s crucial to address the potential risks and considerations associated with each diet. This section provides an informative and straightforward overview of the factors one should be mindful of before adopting either diet.

Carnivore Diet Risks and Considerations: The Carnivore Diet, while simple and potentially beneficial for certain health goals, poses several risks. The most significant is the potential for nutritional deficiencies, especially in vitamins and minerals typically found in plant-based foods, like Vitamin C and fiber. There’s also the concern of high saturated fat intake, which may impact heart health, although this is subject to ongoing debate in the nutrition community. Furthermore, the exclusion of carbohydrates can lead to short-term side effects like fatigue, headaches, and constipation, commonly known as the “keto flu.”

Keto Diet Risks and Considerations: The Keto Diet, despite its popularity, is not without risks. Maintaining a state of ketosis requires strict adherence to macronutrient ratios, which can be challenging and unsustainable for some. There’s a risk of nutrient deficiencies if the diet is not well-planned, particularly in terms of fiber and certain vitamins. The diet may also exacerbate existing kidney problems due to the increased workload from processing protein and fats. Additionally, the initial phase of the diet can lead to the “keto flu,” with symptoms like nausea, dizziness, and fatigue.

Comparing the Risks: Both diets require careful consideration to avoid nutritional deficiencies. The Carnivore Diet’s lack of plant-based nutrients contrasts with the Keto Diet, which allows for a more varied intake but requires careful macronutrient management. It’s important for individuals considering these diets to consult healthcare professionals, especially those with pre-existing health conditions.

Impact on Physical Performance

Evaluating the “Carnivore Diet vs Keto” in terms of their impact on physical performance is essential, especially for athletes or those with an active lifestyle.

Carnivore Diet and Physical Performance: The Carnivore Diet’s high protein intake is beneficial for muscle building and repair, which is crucial for anyone engaged in regular strength training. However, the absence of carbohydrates – a primary energy source for high-intensity activities – might initially lead to reduced endurance and energy levels. Over time, some individuals may adapt to using fats more efficiently for energy, but this can vary greatly from person to person.

Some on the carnivore diet have added berries to help offset the loss of energy if they’ve run into difficulty transitioning to fats for fuel. This moves away from a strict carnivore practice but with any lifestyle, it is best to tailor it to fit within your specific needs depending on your level of physical activity.

Keto Diet and Physical Performance: The Keto Diet is known for its ability to stabilize energy levels, reducing the spikes and crashes often associated with high-carb diets. This can be advantageous for endurance sports. However, the transition period into ketosis can temporarily impact performance, as the body adjusts to using fat instead of carbohydrates for fuel. Once adapted, individuals often report sustained energy levels, which can be beneficial for prolonged physical activities.

For long distance endurance athletes, some individuals have added small portions of potatoes and other fruits (such as apples and pears) to tailor the keto diet to fit their lifestyle. There is no need to be completely rigid with this system to reap the massive benefits, the most important thing is to use the principles to make it work for your specific situation.

Comparing the Two: When comparing the impact on physical performance between the “Carnivore Diet vs Keto,” it’s important to note the potential for flexibility within each diet to support the varying energy requirements of different athletes. While the Carnivore Diet is primarily focused on animal products, some athletes might introduce minimal amounts of certain fruits like berries or even small portions of potatoes to meet higher energy demands, especially in high-intensity sports. This adaptation, though not strictly within the traditional framework of the diet, can provide necessary carbohydrates for energy.

Similarly, the Keto Diet, known for its low-carb approach, does allow for some inclusion of carbohydrates in the form of berries, other low-glycemic fruits, and vegetables like potatoes, particularly for athletes. This flexibility can be crucial for those engaging in more strenuous activities, as it provides a readily available energy source while still maintaining the overall principles of the diet.

In both “Carnivore Diet vs Keto,” the key is to balance the core principles of the diet with the individual energy needs of the athlete. This customization ensures that the dietary approach supports their specific activity levels and performance goals, making each diet adaptable to a wider range of physical demands.

Scientific Evidence and Studies

In the debate of “Carnivore Diet vs Keto,” examining the scientific evidence and studies behind each diet is crucial for an informed perspective.

Carnivore Diet Scientific Evidence: The Carnivore Diet, being relatively new in the realm of popular diets, has limited direct scientific studies. However, research on diets high in protein and low in carbohydrates can offer some insights. Studies suggest that high protein intake can be beneficial for weight loss, muscle mass retention, and satiety.

There is one major recent study published December 2021, which directly references the carnivore diet and concluded, “contrary to common expectations, adults consuming a carnivore diet experienced few adverse effects and instead reported health benefits and high satisfaction.”

However, due to the lack of extensive scientific studies specifically on this diet, some insights can be drawn from other studies on diets high in protein and low in carbohydrates. For instance:

  1. High Protein Diets and Satiety: A study in the “American Journal of Clinical Nutrition” (Weigle et al., 2005) showed that high-protein diets can lead to reduced calorie intake due to increased satiety.
  2. Low Carbohydrate Diets and Health Outcomes: Research by Yancy et al. (2004), published in “Annals of Internal Medicine,” examining low carbohydrate diets (not exclusively carnivore) indicated improvements in body weight and certain metabolic markers.

Keto Diet Scientific Evidence: The Keto Diet has been more extensively studied, particularly in the context of weight loss and managing epilepsy. Research indicates that the Keto Diet can be effective for rapid weight loss and improving markers of metabolic health, such as blood sugar and cholesterol levels. It’s also well-documented in its therapeutic effects on reducing the frequency of seizures in epileptic patients.

For the Keto Diet, specific studies can be cited:

  1. The Potential Health Benefits of the Ketogenic Diet: A Narrative Review: A study published in the “National Library of Medicine” (May 13,2021) demonstrated that a keto diet has helped patients with diabetes reduce their HbA1c and reduce the need for insulin and evidence also suggests that eating a high-fat diet improves lipid profiles by lowering low-density lipoprotein (LDL), increasing high-density lipoprotein (HDL), and lowering triglycerides (TG)
  2. Weight Loss and Metabolic Health: A study published in the journal “Nutrition & Metabolism” (Volek et al., 2004) demonstrated that a ketogenic diet can result in significant weight loss and improved triglyceride levels.

Comparing the Two: Both diets demonstrate benefits in weight management and metabolic health improvement in the short term. The Keto Diet, with its broader body of research, offers a more scientifically-backed approach. In contrast, the Carnivore Diet, while showing potential benefits, still lacks extensive scientific study and validation.

Cost Comparison

A practical aspect of the “Carnivore Diet vs Keto” discussion involves comparing the cost of adhering to each diet. This section aims to provide a straightforward analysis of the financial implications of following either diet.

Carnivore Diet Cost Considerations: The Carnivore Diet primarily consists of meat, fish, eggs, and some dairy products. The cost can vary significantly based on the types of meats chosen (e.g., grass-fed beef is typically more expensive than grain-fed) and the source of the products (local butcher vs. supermarket). Since the diet is exclusively animal-based, there’s little spending on fruits, vegetables, grains, or processed foods, which can offset some of the costs. However, a diet consisting largely of high-quality meats can be more expensive than a more varied diet that includes plant-based foods.

Keto Diet Cost Considerations: The Keto Diet requires a variety of food items including meats, fats (like oils and avocados), low-carb vegetables, nuts, and seeds. Specialty keto products, such as sugar substitutes and low-carb flours, can add to the cost. While the diet includes more expensive items like meat and cheese, the inclusion of vegetables and other plant-based foods can provide more flexibility to balance the overall cost. Keto-friendly snacks and prepared foods, though convenient, can also increase the diet’s cost if relied upon regularly.

Comparing the Two: In comparing “Carnivore Diet vs Keto,” the Carnivore Diet may initially seem more expensive due to its heavy reliance on meat. However, the absence of processed foods and snacks can make it more cost-effective than it first appears. The Keto Diet, with its diverse food items, can be tailored to a wider range of budgets, but specialty items and keto substitutes may add to the overall expense.

Community and Support

When exploring “Carnivore Diet vs Keto,” the aspect of community and support plays a significant role in the success and sustainability of these diets.

Carnivore Diet Community and Support: The Carnivore Diet, while newer in the diet scene, has a growing community. Online forums, social media groups, and blogs are increasingly popular, where enthusiasts share experiences, recipes, and tips. A couple of excellent proponents of the carnivore diet are Dr. Paul Saladino and Dr. Shawn Baker.

The community support can be invaluable for beginners seeking advice or long-term adherents looking to share their journey. The diet’s simplicity also leads to straightforward advice and shared experiences, which can be especially encouraging for newcomers.

Keto Diet Community and Support: The Keto Diet boasts a large and well-established community, given its longer presence in the mainstream. There are numerous online resources, including websites, forums, social media groups, and countless blogs dedicated to the Keto lifestyle. This extensive community offers a wealth of information, from detailed meal plans to adaptations for various health needs. Additionally, the availability of keto-specific products and the diet’s popularity make it easier to find support and resources in both online and offline settings.

Comparing the Two: In comparing “Carnivore Diet vs Keto,” the Keto Diet has a more extensive support system due to its longer-standing presence and broader appeal. However, the Carnivore Diet’s community, though smaller, is noted for its passion and commitment, providing strong peer support. Both communities offer unique benefits, whether it’s the vast array of resources available to Keto dieters or the focused, shared experience within the Carnivore Diet community.

Personalization and Flexibility

In the comparison of “Carnivore Diet vs Keto,” understanding each diet’s capacity for personalization and flexibility is important for those considering which to adopt.

Carnivore Diet Personalization and Flexibility: The Carnivore Diet is inherently restrictive, focusing solely on animal products. This limitation means there’s less room for personalization in terms of food variety. However, within the animal product spectrum, individuals can choose from a range of meats, fish, and dairy, depending on personal taste and tolerance. The diet is less flexible when it comes to accommodating eating out or social dining situations, as it strictly excludes plant-based foods. For those with specific dietary preferences or restrictions, such as lean meats or dairy intolerance, the diet can be adjusted accordingly.

Keto Diet Personalization and Flexibility: The Keto Diet offers more flexibility and personalization due to its wider variety of acceptable foods. Individuals can tailor their diet to include a balance of animal products, low-carb vegetables, nuts, and seeds. This variety allows for more creativity in meal planning and makes it easier to adapt to different social and dining situations. The diet can also be modified to suit various dietary needs and preferences, such as vegetarian keto or dairy-free keto.

Comparing the Two: When comparing “Carnivore Diet vs Keto” in terms of flexibility, the Keto Diet stands out as the more adaptable option. Its variety of food groups allows for a more personalized approach, catering to different tastes and dietary needs. The Carnivore Diet’s simplicity offers less variety, but it can be appealing for those who prefer a more straightforward, no-frills approach to eating.

Conclusion and Recommendations

In concluding our comparison of the “Carnivore Diet vs Keto,” it’s clear that both diets have their unique attributes and potential benefits, along with specific considerations and challenges. Here are some recommendations to consider when choosing between these two dietary approaches:

  1. Assess Personal Health Goals: Your choice should align with your individual health objectives, whether it’s weight loss, improved metabolic health, or other specific needs.
  2. Consider Lifestyle and Preferences: The practicality of maintaining each diet based on your lifestyle, culinary preferences, and social eating habits is crucial. The Keto Diet may offer more variety and flexibility, while the Carnivore Diet appeals to those who prefer simplicity and are comfortable with a more restrictive approach.
  3. Consult Healthcare Professionals: Before starting either diet, especially if you have pre-existing health conditions, consult with a healthcare provider or a registered dietitian. They can provide personalized advice and ensure the diet aligns with your health needs.
  4. Listen to Your Body: Pay attention to how your body responds to the diet. What works for one person may not work for another. Adjustments might be necessary to find the right balance.
  5. Consider Nutritional Balance: Be mindful of potential nutritional deficiencies. Supplements may be necessary, particularly with the Carnivore Diet, to ensure a well-rounded intake of nutrients.
  6. Think Long-Term: Evaluate the sustainability of your chosen diet. A diet that can be adapted and maintained over time is more likely to lead to long-term success and health benefits.
  7. Stay Informed: As research evolves, so does our understanding of diet and nutrition. Stay informed about the latest studies and recommendations.

In summary, both the Carnivore Diet and Keto Diet offer unique approaches to nutrition and health, each with its own set of benefits and drawbacks. The decision to follow either should be based on thorough personal research, consideration of individual health needs, and professional guidance. Ultimately, the best diet is one that you can maintain healthily and happily in the long term.
